who: People who use switches or voice
takeaways: In one process, do not make people type the same information twice. Fill it in for them, or let them pick it.
The classic fix is a “Same as billing address” checkbox, or a list of addresses they already gave.
It applies within the same process, such as one checkout or application, not across separate visits.
Exceptions: when re-entering is essential, needed for security, or the earlier information is no longer valid.
failures: Shipping and billing addresses both typed in full
An email asked for on step 1 and again on step 4
A review step that clears fields when people go back to edit
check: Map every field in the flow and look for the same information asked twice.
Step backward and forward through the prototype. Does entered data survive?
For each repeat, choose auto-fill or a selectable option, and draw it.

quiz.question: A five-step application asks for the applicant’s phone number on step 1 and a contact number on step 4. What is the best design?
options: Ask again, so people can confirm it
Pre-fill step 4 with the step 1 number, still editable
quiz.why: Auto-populating meets the rule and keeps the option to give a different number. Removing the question may lose a real need.

spec: Mark each field that reuses earlier data, and name its source step.
Say whether it is pre-filled or offered as a choice, and that it stays editable.
Note any repeat kept on purpose, and which exception it falls under.
review: Where in this flow does the person tell us something twice?
What happens to their data when they press Back?
Is this repeat really for security, or just how the form was built?
tradeoff: Pre-filled data can be wrong for this step, like a work address reused as a delivery address. Pre-fill or offer it, but keep it visible and editable.
system: Build address and contact patterns with a “use a saved or earlier value” option built in.
pitch: Asking for the same thing twice feels careless to every customer, and blocks some of them.
